title: Taking 'rights' apart
subtitle: Hohfeld's analytical scheme of fundamental legal conceptions
objectives: State Hohfeld's eight fundamental legal conceptions and pair each into its correlative and its jural opposite
Explain why loose, undifferentiated use of the word 'right' produces muddled legal reasoning, and identify which Hohfeldian conception a given legal claim is really asserting
Apply the full scheme to a concrete dispute — a residential tenancy — correctly identifying each party's claim-rights, privileges, powers and immunities and their correlatives

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hohfeld, 'Some Fundamental Legal Conceptions as Applied in Judicial Reasoning' (1913) 23 Yale LJ 16
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the eight conceptions and the correlative/opposite squares

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hohfeld, 'Fundamental Legal Conceptions as Applied in Judicial Reasoning' (1917) 26 Yale LJ 710
leadingAuthorities.role: Develops and refines the scheme, with further worked judicial examples
Used in this lesson as a concrete illustration of a statutory disability on a landlord's power of self-help eviction

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Hohfeld's scheme has no 'side' to take — it's a piece of analytical machinery, not a theory of what the law should be. This lesson tests whether you can use it precisely: correctly sorting a real dispute into claim-rights, privileges, powers and immunities, not just reciting the eight labels.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the eight conceptions. This test pool is weighted towards applying them to a live scenario — expect a lease or an easement, not a list to complete.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Parts 1–3 and get the two squares (correlatives and opposites) solid before Part 5's worked example asks you to use all eight together.

overview.hook: A landlord tells a tenant: 'I have a right to enter your flat whenever I like.' A trade union official tells an employer: 'Workers have a right to strike.' A company tells a regulator: 'We have a right to set our own prices.' Three uses of the word 'right' — and, on Wesley Hohfeld's analysis, at least three different legal ideas smuggled under one label, only one of which necessarily imposes a duty on anyone else. This lesson gives you the tool to take any of those sentences apart.

parts.heading: The trouble with 'right'
parts.voice: argumentative — diagnoses the problem before offering the cure
body: Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld, writing in 1913, made a complaint that sounds almost too simple to matter: lawyers, judges and legislators use the word 'right' to mean at least four analytically different things, and treat them as interchangeable. The result, he argued, is not just imprecise language but genuinely muddled legal reasoning — judges sliding from one sense of 'right' to another within a single argument, and reaching conclusions that a more careful vocabulary would expose as non sequiturs.

Consider three claims that all use the word 'right': 'I have a right that you not trespass on my land' (this generates a duty on you); 'I have a right to walk across my own field' (this is really just an absence of any duty stopping me — it generates no duty on anyone else); 'I have a right to sell my house' (this is really a power to change legal relations by my own act, such as by signing a contract). Only the first of these creates a duty in someone else. Calling all three 'rights' obscures that difference.

Hohfeld's project was to replace this single overloaded word with eight precise, narrower terms — four pairs of correlatives, arranged so that asserting one position in a pair automatically tells you what position the other party holds.

components.definition: In Hohfeld's scheme, a position held by one party that necessarily entails a matching position in another party — for example, a claim-right in A necessarily entails a duty in B. The two are two descriptions of the same single legal relation, seen from each side.

interaction.prompt: Does saying 'I have a right to walk across my own field' necessarily create a duty owed to me by anyone else?
options: No — on Hohfeld's analysis this is really a privilege (absence of a duty not to act), which generates no duty on anyone else
Yes — every use of the word 'right' automatically creates a duty in someone else
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. That's exactly Hohfeld's point — this everyday use of 'right' is really a privilege, correlative only to others' 'no-right' to stop you, not to any duty owed to you.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. This everyday sense of 'right' — a mere liberty to act — is what Hohfeld calls a privilege, and a privilege does not generate a duty in anyone else. Only a claim-right does that.

parts.heading: The first square: claim-right/duty and privilege/no-right
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: The first pair is the one lawyers already use fairly precisely: a claim-right in A is correlative to a duty in B. If A has a claim-right that B not enter A's land, B is under a duty not to enter. Neither position can exist without the other — they are two names for the same legal relation.

The second pair is where everyday usage goes wrong. A privilege (sometimes called a liberty) is simply the absence of a duty not to act. If A has a privilege to walk across A's own field, that just means A is under no duty to refrain — and the correlative position in everyone else is a 'no-right': they have no claim-right that A refrain from walking there. Crucially, a privilege generates no duty in anyone else at all.

Confusing claim-right with privilege is the single most common Hohfeldian error. Saying 'I have a right to say what I like' usually describes a privilege (freedom from a duty of silence) — it does not, by itself, impose any duty on your audience to listen, agree, or provide you a platform.

components.label: Square one: claim-right/duty and privilege/no-right
points: Claim-right (A) ↔ Duty (B): A can demand B act or refrain; B must comply
Privilege (A) ↔ No-right (B): A is free to act or not act; B has no claim to stop A
A claim-right restricts someone else's freedom; a privilege only describes the absence of a restriction on you
Test: does asserting the position impose a duty on anyone else? If yes, it's a claim-right; if no, it's only a privilege

interaction.prompt: Which of the following pairs is a jural OPPOSITE in Hohfeld's scheme, rather than a jural correlative?
options: Right (claim) and duty
Privilege and duty
Power and liability
Immunity and disability
interaction.trapExplanation: Privilege and duty are opposites — having a privilege to do X means you are not under a duty not to do X — not correlatives. The four correlative pairs are right/duty, privilege/no-right, power/liability and immunity/disability.

parts.heading: The second square: power/liability and immunity/disability
parts.voice: structural — extends the reference framework to the dynamic conceptions
body: The first square describes static positions — who must do what, right now. The second square describes the ability to change those positions. A power is the legal ability to alter someone's legal relations by your own voluntary act — making a will, serving notice, signing a contract, exercising a break clause. The correlative position in whoever is affected is a liability: susceptibility to having your legal position changed by another's exercise of their power, whether or not you agree.

An immunity is the mirror image at one remove: freedom from having your legal relations changed by another's purported power. If A is immune from B's purported power to do something, B's attempt simply fails to change anything — B is under a disability, the correlative position, meaning B lacks the legal ability to bring about that change at all.

Note carefully: 'liability' here is a neutral, technical term — it doesn't mean 'being at fault'. It simply names the position of anyone whose legal relations can be validly altered by someone else's power, for better or worse.

components.label: Square two: power/liability and immunity/disability
points: Power (A) ↔ Liability (B): A can validly change B's legal position by A's own act; B is subject to that change
Immunity (A) ↔ Disability (B): A is protected from having A's legal position changed by B; B lacks the power to do it
'Liability' is a neutral technical term here, not a synonym for fault or wrongdoing
Test: does the position describe the ability (or inability) to change legal relations by one's own act? If yes, you're in the power/liability or immunity/disability square, not the static square

interaction.prompt: In this passage adapted from Hohfeld's 1913 article, highlight the sentence that defines a legal power.
interaction.passage: A change in a given legal relation may result from some superadded fact or group of facts over which the party has no control, or, alternatively, from the existence of an ability on the part of some person to bring about such a change by his own voluntary act. The person having that ability is said to have the power to change the legal relations of another.
interaction.ratioSentence: The person having that ability is said to have the power to change the legal relations of another.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the definition Hohfeld is building towards — a power is precisely the ability to change another's legal relations by one's own voluntary act.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the sentence that names the ability to change another's legal relations by one's own act — that's Hohfeld's definition of a power.

parts.heading: Putting the squares together
parts.voice: reflective — consolidates before the worked example
body: Hohfeld's eight conceptions form two independent squares, and it's worth being explicit about how they relate. Within each square, the horizontal pairs are correlatives (right/duty, privilege/no-right, power/liability, immunity/disability) — two sides of the same coin, always found together. The diagonal pairs across each square are jural opposites (right/no-right, privilege/duty, power/disability, immunity/liability) — if you have one, by definition you cannot simultaneously have the other, in the same respect, against the same party.

It's tempting to think the eight conceptions reduce to two ideas dressed up eight ways, but that misses Hohfeld's real payoff: a huge amount of confused legal argument trades on sliding between squares without noticing — treating a mere privilege as though it generated a duty, or a power as though it were a claim-right. Naming the conception precisely is what exposes the slide.

Two conceptions do the least intuitive work and are worth fixing especially firmly: immunity (a legal exemption from a specific power someone else would otherwise have) and disability (the correlative gap in that other person's abilities). These are not about physical or personal incapacity — they describe a purely legal inability to alter someone's position.

components.definition: In Hohfeld's scheme, two positions that cannot both be held by the same party, in the same respect, at the same time — for example, having a claim-right that X happen is the opposite of having no-right that X happen. Opposites sit on the diagonal of each square; correlatives sit on the horizontal.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that 'right' and 'privilege' mean exactly the same thing in Hohfeld's scheme?
sliderLabels: Same thing — right and privilege are interchangeable
Different — a right (claim) is correlative to a duty; a privilege (liberty) is correlative to a no-right
interaction.explanation: They are analytically distinct: a claim-right is always matched by someone else's duty; a privilege is simply the absence of a duty not to act, matched by the other party's absence of a right to stop you — no duty on anyone is generated by a mere privilege.

parts.heading: Worked example: a residential tenancy
parts.voice: case-narrative — applies the full scheme to one running scenario
body: Priya rents a flat from her landlord, Robert. Under the tenancy, Priya has a claim-right to live in and use the flat undisturbed; correlatively, Robert is under a duty not to enter without notice or otherwise interfere with her occupation. That's the first correlative pair: claim-right and duty.

Priya also has a privilege to use the flat in the ordinary ways the tenancy permits — cooking, hosting guests, decorating within the lease's terms. This privilege is correlative to Robert having no-right to stop those ordinary uses; but note it generates no duty on Robert to, say, help Priya decorate — a privilege only ever removes a duty from the privilege-holder, it doesn't impose one on anyone else.

Separately, Robert's tenancy agreement gives him a contractual power to terminate the tenancy for rent arrears by serving a valid notice. The moment he validly exercises it, Priya's legal position changes automatically — she is under a liability to have her tenancy altered by Robert's unilateral act, whether or not she agrees. But Robert cannot lawfully evict Priya himself, by his own hand, without a court order: s 3 of the Protection from Eviction Act 1977 removes that self-help option for most residential tenancies. In Hohfeldian terms, the statute puts Robert under a disability as to self-help eviction, correlative to an immunity Priya holds against being evicted other than through the court.

components.text: Where any premises have been let as a dwelling under a tenancy which is neither a statutorily protected tenancy nor an excluded tenancy... it shall not be lawful for the owner to enforce against the occupier, otherwise than by proceedings in court, his right to recover possession of the premises.
elements: Removes the landlord's power of self-help repossession for most residential tenancies
Substitutes a requirement of court proceedings before possession can be lawfully enforced
In Hohfeldian terms: a statutory disability on the landlord, correlative to a statutory immunity for the occupier

interaction.prompt: Robert serves a valid contractual notice terminating Priya's tenancy for rent arrears, then — frustrated at the delay of going to court — changes the locks while Priya is at work. Analyse Robert's legal position using Hohfeld's scheme.
factsToOrder: Robert validly exercises his contractual power to terminate by serving notice
Priya's tenancy position changes as a result — she is under a liability to that change
The Protection from Eviction Act 1977, s 3 puts Robert under a disability as to self-help repossession
Robert changes the locks himself, without a court order

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student drags facts into Application and writes the Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, applies the facts and writes the Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Robert's act of changing the locks is something Hohfeld's scheme shows he had the legal ability to do, even though his power to terminate the tenancy was validly exercised.
modelAnswer.rule: A valid exercise of a power changes the other party's legal relations (here, ending the tenancy), but a power to terminate a tenancy is analytically distinct from a power to enforce repossession by one's own act. Section 3 PEA 1977 places residential landlords under a disability as to self-help repossession, correlative to the occupier's statutory immunity, regardless of whether the underlying tenancy has validly ended.
modelAnswer.application: Robert's notice validly exercised his contractual power, changing Priya's position (a liability she was subject to) and ending the tenancy. But that only settles the first square. Changing the locks himself is an attempted exercise of a different ability — self-help repossession — which s 3 removes from Robert entirely. Because Robert is under a statutory disability here, his act does not validly change Priya's legal position with respect to possession; Priya's immunity means only a court order can do that.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The tenancy has validly ended, but Robert's self-help lock change is not a valid exercise of any power he holds — it is unlawful under s 3, precisely because Hohfeldian disability, not merely bad manners, is what stands in his way.

testPool.prompt: Name Hohfeld's four pairs of jural correlatives.
testPool.modelAnswer: Claim-right and duty; privilege (liberty) and no-right; power and liability; immunity and disability.

testPool.prompt: State, in one sentence, the problem Hohfeld identified with how lawyers and courts use the word 'right'.
acceptableAnswers: it's used loosely to mean claim, privilege, power or immunity interchangeably, which causes muddled reasoning
testPool.modelAnswer: Lawyers and courts routinely use 'right' to mean at least four analytically distinct things — a claim, a privilege, a power, or an immunity — and treating them as interchangeable produces confused, sometimes fallacious, legal reasoning.

testPool.prompt: Is a 'privilege' in Hohfeld's sense the same as a 'claim-right'?
options: No — a privilege is freedom from a duty not to act, correlative to another's no-right; a claim-right is correlative to another's duty
Yes — they are simply two names for the same legal position

testPool.prompt: Which of the following pairs is a jural OPPOSITE in Hohfeld's scheme, rather than a jural correlative?
options: Immunity and disability
Power and disability
Power and liability
Right (claim) and duty
testPool.trapExplanation: Power and disability are opposites — you cannot simultaneously hold a power and lack it (a disability) with respect to the same act — whereas immunity/disability, power/liability, and right/duty are the correlative pairs.

testPool.prompt: Put these reasoning steps in the order Hohfeld's method requires when someone loosely asserts 'I have a right to do X'.
items: Identify which of the four Hohfeldian conceptions is actually being claimed (claim-right, privilege, power or immunity)
Identify the correlative position this creates in the other party
Check the claim against the facts to see whether that correlative genuinely exists
Restate the original assertion in precise Hohfeldian terms

testPool.prompt: Read this extract from the Protection from Eviction Act 1977, s 3(1): 'Where any premises have been let as a dwelling under a tenancy which is neither a statutorily protected tenancy nor an excluded tenancy... it shall not be lawful for the owner to enforce... his right to recover possession... otherwise than by proceedings in court.' In Hohfeldian terms, what does this provision principally do to the landlord's position?
options: It removes the landlord's ability to repossess by self-help, replacing it with a disability that can only be overcome via court proceedings
It grants the landlord an immunity from being sued by the tenant
It creates a new privilege for the tenant to stay rent-free

testPool.prompt: In this passage adapted from Hohfeld's 1913 article, highlight the sentence that captures why precise use of legal terms matters to judicial reasoning.
testPool.passage: So long as courts and lawyers use the single term 'right' to cover claims, liberties, powers and immunities indiscriminately, arguments will continue to trade, often unnoticed, on the ambiguity — a conclusion valid for one of these conceptions being silently applied as though it held for another. Only by naming each conception separately can such slippage be exposed and avoided.
testPool.ratioSentence: Only by naming each conception separately can such slippage be exposed and avoided.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario illustrates a Hohfeldian power being exercised?
testPool.scenarioA: An employer, under the express terms of an at-will contract, gives an employee notice terminating the contract, thereby altering the employee's legal position from 'employed' to 'former employee'.
testPool.scenarioB: A neighbour is simply annoyed that another neighbour parks a car, slightly inconveniently, on a public street they are both entitled to use.
testPool.explanation: A shows a power in Hohfeld's sense: a unilateral act (giving notice) that itself changes the legal relations between the parties, with the employee correlatively under a liability to have that change made. B involves no exercise of any legal power — at most a privilege each neighbour holds to use the street, subject to each other's absence of a right to stop lawful use.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that best illustrates a claim-right correlative to a duty.
testPool.scenarioText: Under a residential tenancy agreement, Priya is entitled to live in and use the flat undisturbed. Her landlord, Robert, is not permitted to enter without notice or interfere with her occupation. Separately, Robert holds a contractual power to terminate the tenancy for rent arrears by serving a valid notice, though he cannot lawfully evict Priya himself without first obtaining a court order under the Protection from Eviction Act 1977.
tappableSpans: entitled to live in and use the flat undisturbed
not permitted to enter without notice or interfere with her occupation
Robert holds a contractual power to terminate the tenancy
cannot lawfully evict Priya himself without first obtaining a court order
testPool.correctSpan: not permitted to enter without notice or interfere with her occupation
testPool.explanation: That's the duty side of the claim-right/duty correlative — Priya's claim-right to undisturbed occupation exists precisely because Robert is under a correlative duty not to interfere. The power to terminate and the disability on self-help eviction are different Hohfeldian conceptions illustrated elsewhere in the scenario.

testPool.prompt: In the same scenario, tap the fact that illustrates Robert being under a Hohfeldian disability.
testPool.scenarioText: Under a residential tenancy agreement, Priya is entitled to live in and use the flat undisturbed. Her landlord, Robert, is not permitted to enter without notice or interfere with her occupation. Separately, Robert holds a contractual power to terminate the tenancy for rent arrears by serving a valid notice, though he cannot lawfully evict Priya himself without first obtaining a court order under the Protection from Eviction Act 1977.
tappableSpans: entitled to live in and use the flat undisturbed
not permitted to enter without notice or interfere with her occupation
Robert holds a contractual power to terminate the tenancy
cannot lawfully evict Priya himself without first obtaining a court order
testPool.correctSpan: cannot lawfully evict Priya himself without first obtaining a court order
testPool.explanation: This is a disability: statute removes Robert's ability to change Priya's legal position (from tenant to evicted former-tenant) by his own act; he lacks the legal power to do it himself, correlative to Priya's immunity from self-help eviction.

testPool.prompt: Robert serves a valid notice terminating the tenancy for arrears, as his contract permits. In Hohfeldian terms, what is Priya's position the moment that valid notice is served?
options: Priya is under a liability — her legal position changes as a direct result of Robert's exercise of his power, whether or not she agrees
Priya retains an immunity that blocks any change to her tenancy
Nothing changes until Priya herself consents to leave
testPool.explanation: A valid exercise of a power changes the other party's legal relations directly — that susceptibility to having one's position changed by another's power is exactly what Hohfeld calls a liability. Priya's tenancy position changes on service of a valid notice, whether or not she agrees (though other protections, like the PEA 1977, control how any resulting possession can actually be enforced).

testPool.prompt: A first-year student says: 'Priya has an immunity from Robert's notice because she doesn't want to leave.' Is this correct in Hohfeldian terms?
options: No — an immunity is a specific legal exemption from a particular power recognised by law (such as PEA 1977's control on self-help eviction), not simply a personal wish to resist a lawful exercise of power
Yes — wanting to stay is itself an immunity
testPool.explanation: Immunity is a technical Hohfeldian position: freedom from having one's legal relations changed by another's purported power, recognised by law — it isn't generated by mere personal preference. Priya has no immunity from a validly exercised termination power; what she does have is a statutory immunity from Robert enforcing possession except through the court.

testPool.prompt: A dominant landowner, D, has an express, validly registered easement (a right of way) across a neighbour's land, S, to reach the public road. S builds a fence blocking the path. Applying Hohfeld's scheme, analyse the legal relations between D and S.
factsToOrder: D holds a validly registered express easement (right of way) over S's land
S has built a fence blocking the path
D wants to know whether S's conduct breaches any Hohfeldian duty owed to D

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether S's obstruction of the path breaches a Hohfeldian duty correlative to D's claim-right under the easement.
modelAnswer.rule: A valid easement gives the dominant owner a claim-right to use the path; the servient owner is under a correlative duty not to obstruct that use. This is distinct from any question of power (either party's ability to vary or extinguish the easement) or immunity (protection from unilateral extinguishment).
modelAnswer.application: D's registered easement establishes a claim-right to pass over S's land. S's fence directly interferes with that use, and is therefore a breach of S's correlative duty not to obstruct D's right of way. Nothing here involves the exercise of a power — S has not purported to change the legal relation, for example by validly terminating the easement — S has simply broken the duty already attached to D's existing claim-right.
modelAnswer.conclusion: S is in breach of the duty correlative to D's claim-right; D can seek a remedy, such as an injunction, to enforce that duty, without needing to show any power or immunity issue.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that 'liability' in Hohfeld's scheme means the same thing as 'being at fault'?
sliderLabels: Different — liability is a neutral term for being subject to another's power, regardless of fault
testPool.explanation: Hohfeldian liability is purely structural: it names anyone whose legal position can be validly changed by someone else's power. It carries no implication of wrongdoing — an employee subject to a lawful dismissal power, or a tenant subject to a lawful termination power, is 'liable' in this sense with no fault involved at all.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake is pairing correlatives and opposites incorrectly — remembering that right/duty and privilege/no-right are correlatives, while right/no-right and privilege/duty are opposites, is worth the extra care it takes.
